items.followUp: Define stress and state its S.I. unit.

rubric.why: Young’s modulus is defined as the ratio of stress to strain.
rubric.description: States the ratio of stress to strain.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct ratio.

rubric.why: The ratio is defined for a material within its elastic limit.
rubric.description: Specifies that the definition applies within the elastic limit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the elastic-limit condition.

modelAnswer: Young’s modulus is the ratio of stress to strain in a material, provided the material is within its elastic limit.
Young’s modulus = stress / strain.
Its S.I. unit is pascal (Pa).

items.followUp: A 2 kg object moving at 8 m s⁻¹ is brought to rest in 4 s. Find the force acting on it.

rubric.why: The mass and initial velocity are needed to solve the problem.
rubric.description: Identifies the mass and initial velocity in S.I. units.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the given values.

rubric.why: Acceleration is calculated from the change in velocity over time.
rubric.description: Uses the acceleration formula.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct formula.

rubric.why: The acceleration is negative because the body is slowing down.
rubric.description: Finds the acceleration as −5 m s⁻².
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correct substitution and acceleration.

rubric.why: Newton’s second law gives the stopping force, whose direction is opposite to the motion.
rubric.description: Finds the force as 25 N opposite to the motion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for applying F = ma and 1 mark for the correct magnitude and direction.

modelAnswer: Given: m = 5 kg, u = 10 m s⁻¹, v = 0 m s⁻¹, t = 2 s.
Formula: a = (v − u) / t.
Substitution: a = (0 − 10) / 2 = −5 m s⁻².
Formula: F = ma.
Substitution: F = 5 × (−5) = −25 N.
The required force has magnitude 25 N and acts opposite to the motion.

items.followUp: Derive the formula for the kinetic energy of a body of mass m moving with speed v.

rubric.why: Kinetic energy is the energy associated with motion.
rubric.description: Defines kinetic energy as the energy a body possesses due to its motion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the definition.

rubric.why: The derivation begins with work done and Newton’s second law.
rubric.description: Uses work done W = Fs and relates force to acceleration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the work and force relations.

rubric.why: The displacement is related to the final speed using the equation of motion, starting from rest.
rubric.description: Uses the equation of motion to obtain displacement for a body starting from rest.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the relevant equation and use of u = 0.

rubric.why: Substituting displacement into work gives the required kinetic-energy expression.
rubric.description: Derives the final formula for kinetic energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct derivation result.

modelAnswer: Kinetic energy is the energy possessed by a body due to its motion.
Work done, W = Fs, and F = ma.
For a body starting from rest, u = 0 and v² − u² = 2as, so s = v² / 2a.
Therefore, KE = W = Fs = (ma)(v² / 2a) = ½mv².

items.followUp: A 20 cm spanner is used to apply a perpendicular force of 150 N to a nut. Find the torque.

rubric.why: The lever arm must be expressed in S.I. units.
rubric.description: Converts the spanner length to 0.15 m.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct conversion.

rubric.why: Torque is the product of force and perpendicular distance from the pivot.
rubric.description: States the torque relation and substitutes the given values with units.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the formula and 1 mark for correct substitution.

rubric.why: The force and lever arm give a torque of 30 N m.
rubric.description: Calculates and states the torque with its S.I. unit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the numerical result and 1 mark for the unit.

modelAnswer: Given: F = 200 N, d = 15 cm = 0.15 m.
Formula: torque, τ = Fd, where d is the perpendicular distance from the pivot.
Substitution: τ = 200 N × 0.15 m.
Answer: τ = 30 N m.

items.followUp: A wooden block has dimensions 30 cm × 10 cm × 4 cm and a mass of 600 g. Find its density in S.I. units.

rubric.why: Mass and dimensions are converted to S.I. units before calculating density.
rubric.description: Correctly converts the mass and block dimensions to S.I. units.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the conversions.

rubric.why: The block’s volume is the product of its dimensions, and density is mass divided by volume.
rubric.description: Finds the volume and uses the density formula.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the volume and 1 mark for the formula.

rubric.why: Dividing 0.85 kg by 0.002 m³ gives the density in S.I. units.
rubric.description: Calculates the density and gives its S.I. unit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correct substitution/result and 1 mark for the unit.

modelAnswer: Given: m = 850 g = 0.850 kg.
Dimensions: 40 cm = 0.40 m, 10 cm = 0.10 m, 5 cm = 0.05 m.
Formula: density, ρ = m / V.
Substitution: ρ = 0.850 kg / 0.002 m³ = 425 kg m⁻³.
Answer: the density of the wood is 425 kg m⁻³.

items.followUp: What is the least count of a vernier caliper?

rubric.why: Least count describes the smallest measurement an instrument can measure accurately.
rubric.description: Defines least count as the smallest measurement an instrument can measure accurately.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the definition.

rubric.why: For a screw gauge, least count is calculated from the pitch and circular-scale divisions.
rubric.description: Gives the screw-gauge least-count relation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct formula.

modelAnswer: The least count of a screw gauge is the smallest length it can measure accurately.
Least count = pitch of the screw / number of divisions on the circular scale.
